column4: The boat belongs to poor people who work at sea, showing that “poor” can describe unmet need even when the poor possess a productive asset.
Asked what should be spent, the answer is the surplus beyond need, giving the section's idea of sufficiency a practical threshold.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended completely, because either extreme ends in blame or destitution; spending is calibrated around enoughness.
The servants neither squander nor stint, but keep spending between those extremes, directly expressing wealth governed by measure rather than acquisitive fear.
Sacrificial food is to be given to ٱلْبَآئِسَ ٱلْفَقِيرَ, joining bodily nourishment to an emphatic description of the poor person's distress.
The sacrificial animals feed both the content or non-asking poor person and the one who approaches to ask, refining the section's poor-as-sā'il category.
The command to listen, obey, and spend is joined to rescue from one's own shuhh, directly naming the inward greed that can survive material plenty.
Property is called a means of support established by God; dependents are to be fed, clothed, and addressed kindly from it, uniting material sufficiency with humane speech.
A father must provide a nursing mother's food and clothing reasonably, while no soul is burdened beyond capacity; household provision is fitted to means and need.
A divorced woman receives provision according to the affluent person's capacity and the constrained person's capacity, making rich and poor subject to a measured duty.
After calling for a good loan, the verse says God constricts and expands, locating both material straitness and abundance in the giver to whom all return.
God effaces usury and makes charities grow, opposing acquisitive increase to the kind of giving through which wealth truly bears fruit.
People do not attain true goodness until they spend from what they love, making prized property into khayr only through release rather than possession.
Charity taken from people's property purifies and causes growth, answering the section's concern with wealth's clean source and use.
Religious authorities consume people's property wrongfully and hoard gold and silver instead of spending it, combining corrupt acquisition with refusal to answer need.
The hoarded metal is heated and used to brand its owners, turning stored wealth into the bodily mark of the greed named in 9:34.
People of bounty and means must continue giving to kin, the needy, and emigrants and must pardon, so abundance is defined by what it enables them to pass on.
Some people are pleased with the distribution of charity only when they receive a share and angry when they do not, staging need transformed into entitlement rather than contentment.
وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ ذُو ٱلرَّحْمَةِ joins the section's Rabb and ghani roots: the need-free Lord possesses mercy and can replace creatures without depending on them.
God is هُوَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ and owns all in heaven and earth, so the two definitions of richness—absence of need and possession—coincide fully in Him.
God is rich beyond people's need, yet approves gratitude rather than disbelief, separating the giver's independence from the receiver's duty to acknowledge blessing.
People reject the messengers and turn away, while وَّٱسْتَغْنَى ٱللَّهُ; the reflexive “self-sufficiency” that is false for the grasping human is true of God.
After affirming God's ownership of heaven and earth, the verse names Him rich and praiseworthy, grounding independence in universal possession.
People are to eat the lawful, good provision God supplied and thank His niʿmah, joining nourishment, clean provision, and acknowledgment of its source.
People recognize God's niʿmah and then deny it, the reverse of recounting the comfortable livelihood one has received.
Whatever khayr people spend returns fully to them, using “good” for spendable property while directing it toward the needy context completed in 2:273.
Whatever khayr people send ahead for themselves is found with God as better and greater in reward, moving valuable property from present possession to lasting return.
In its immediate context al-khayr names prized horses whose love distracts from remembrance, a concrete property-sense that shows valued possession becoming attachment.
أُو۟لِى ٱلنَّعْمَةِ names affluent people of ease who deny, using the niʿmah root in precisely the section's secondary sense of comfortable living.
The luxurious niʿmah in which Pharaoh's people delighted is among what they leave behind, making comfortable abundance visibly pass away.
The affluent boast of greater wealth and children and infer that they will not be punished; 34:37 rejects possession as spiritual rank.
The garden owner enters while wronging himself and declares that his property will never perish, mistaking present acquisition for lasting sufficiency.
He doubts the Hour and assumes that even a return to God would bring him something better, carrying material entitlement beyond death.
After the garden's loss, no party can help him besides God and he cannot help himself, exposing the social following of 18:34 as failed sufficiency.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, making the hidden giver's power to remove provision decisive before their exclusion of the poor.
Children kept present around the wealthy man add household and social capital to the wealth and ease God says He placed in his hand.
The return is to the Lord, immediately bounding the human's claim in 96:7 that he has become self-sufficient.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are consuming fire into themselves, reversing the former orphan's obligation to make possession serve rather than prey on vulnerability.
The covenant joins kindness to orphans and the needy with speaking good words to people, matching material vulnerability with a non-rebuking manner.
Good conduct is required toward orphans, the needy, near and distant neighbors, companions, and travelers, widening the doorstep encounter with need.
Kin, the needy, and the traveler are to receive their due, presenting held property as containing claims belonging to vulnerable others.
People are told to spend from God's provision before death makes them wish for one more chance to give charity, setting passing possession against its lasting use.
God establishes people on earth and places livelihoods there, yet they give little thanks, tracing means of living to the provider rather than acquisition alone.
God places livelihoods on earth both for people and for creatures they do not provide for, making hidden provision broader than human ownership.
People's provision and what they are promised are said to be in heaven, locating sufficiency beyond the visible holdings in their hands.
People walk the earth and eat from God's provision, so ordinary livelihood is received from a domain made usable by the provider.
Those fearing dispossession are reminded that they were established in a secure sanctuary to which fruits are brought as provision, answering fear of loss with supplied security.
People are asked why they do not spend when the inheritance of heaven and earth belongs to God, denying that temporary custody makes wealth independently theirs.
The good loan to God is multiplied for its giver, turning property released from the hand into greater provision rather than feared loss.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, another direct answer to acquisitive fear that spending diminishes sufficiency.
The deities invoked besides God do not أَغْنَتْ عَنْهُم when the Lord's command arrives, marking false providers as unable to meet decisive need.
Jacob says his protective plan cannot أُغْنِى عَنكُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ, distinguishing prudent means from the one whose decree ultimately suffices.
Abraham asks why his father serves what cannot hear, see, or يُغْنِى عَنكَ شَيْـًٔا, exposing an alleged provider that can supply no need.
No protecting relation can يُغْنِى one person from another on the decisive day, bounding social dependence as a form of sufficiency.
Even marriage to two righteous servants does not يُغْنِيَا the disbelieving wives before God, showing that a household relation cannot confer ultimate sufficiency.
The smoke's shade neither shelters nor يُغْنِى مِنَ ٱللَّهَبِ, extending the agnā-as-suffice sense to a physical provision that fails its basic purpose.
